Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that put my body under stress
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
Going out at night or being outside after dark

issues.item: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
issues.explanation: These three maladaptive strategy items do not form a clinically coherent set on their own. 'Avoid Dreams' and 'Avoid Physical Stress' are trauma-linked avoidance strategies, but 'Compulsive Cleaning' reflects a distinct control/ritualising pattern that is not clearly tied to the same military PTSD presentation in the absence of any supporting trigger, threat, memory, or appraisal items. With no active edges in the formulation, the node should still be internally coherent; here the items suggest different mechanisms (nightmare avoidance, bodily arousal avoidance, and compulsive control rituals) without evidence they belong to the same symptom pattern.

vignette:
Layla is a 21-year-old woman of Lebanese descent who works as a database administrator at a mid-sized logistics firm. She presents with a PCL-5 score of 79, indicating severe posttraumatic stress, and was referred for psychological assessment following a brief disclosure to her primary care physician.

Layla grew up in a military family and spent a formative period of her adolescence living on or near active bases, including an extended stay abroad during a period of heightened conflict. The traumatic event she identifies as central occurred when she was nineteen: a mortar strike near the base housing where she and her mother were residing struck during the night, collapsing part of a neighbouring structure and sending debris through the windows of their unit. The attack happened without warning, in darkness, and in the chaos that followed - the shouting, the dust, the smell of burning - Layla was separated from her mother for nearly two hours before they were reunited. She was uninjured physically, but the hours she spent crouched behind an overturned table, alone, certain she was about to die, left a mark she has not been able to name until recently.

In the months and then years that followed, Layla began organising her life around the edges of that night without fully recognising she was doing so. The most visible pattern is her refusal to go outside after dark. What began as a preference hardened into something closer to a rule. She does not go to her car after sunset without asking a colleague to walk her, and she has declined several evening social invitations, including a team dinner hosted by her manager, citing vague excuses. Her work hours have quietly shifted - she arrives early and leaves before five - and though her colleagues have not commented directly, she is aware that her absence from after-hours events has made her seem distant. The darkness itself, she has come to feel, is not safe. Night is when things happen without warning.

Inside her apartment, a different pattern has taken hold. Layla cleans and reorganises compulsively - her kitchen, her desk, the cables behind her workstation at the office - returning to the same surfaces multiple times in an evening. She cannot always explain why, but the act of ordering her environment seems to hold something at bay. When her desk is arranged precisely, when the files on her server are sorted and labelled, she feels, briefly, that she has some purchase on the world. Her colleagues have noticed the meticulous organisation of her workspace and have remarked on it admiringly, unaware that it functions less as a professional habit than as a kind of ongoing emergency measure.

She also avoids any situation that places her body under physical stress - she has stopped exercising, declines to carry heavy loads, and once left a fire drill partway through because the exertion and the alarm together produced a sensation she found intolerable. The feeling of her own heart rate rising, of her muscles working hard, carries with it an echo of that night: the pounding in her chest as she crouched in the dark, the physical certainty that something terrible was about to happen to her body. She does not think of this consciously in those terms, but she has learned to interpret physical arousal as a warning sign, and she avoids it accordingly.

What finally brought Layla to seek help was a moment at work three weeks ago. She was running a late query - the office empty, the building quiet - when the lights in her section switched to their automatic dim setting. In the sudden near-darkness, with the hum of the servers around her, she felt something she could not manage with cleaning or early departures or careful schedules. She sat at her desk for a long time afterward, not moving. She is not sure what she is most afraid of in coming to treatment - perhaps that nothing will change, or perhaps that something will, and she will have to feel what she has spent two years arranging her life not to feel.
